analysis.one_liner: Requires most long freight trains to be run by a two-person crew.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee until the two-year session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe Freight Act would have required the big Class I freight railroads to put at least two certified crew members — a conductor and an engineer — on most freight trains operating on main line track. Exceptions existed for yard tracks, helper locomotives, short moves, and operations already running with one person, but none of those exceptions applied to trains carrying hazardous materials or trains longer than 7,500 feet. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Railroad workers, who would gain a second crew member on the train for safety and workload support, and the communities along freight routes, especially towns near tracks carrying flammable, toxic, or explosive cargo.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Class I railroads to staff main line freight trains with at least one certified conductor and one certified engineer, so a crew member can respond to failures, malfunctions, or emergencies without a single operator trying to run and watch the train alone.

Bars the exceptions from applying to high-hazard trains (20+ flammable tank cars, poisonous-by-inhalation cargo, nuclear materials, or explosives) or to trains 7,500 feet or longer, meaning the most dangerous and longest trains would always carry two people.

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads, which would face added staffing costs; those costs could partly show up in shipping rates for goods carried by rail.

drawbacks.text: The grandfather clause lets any operation already running with fewer than two people keep doing so unless the Transportation Secretary finds it unsafe, so the bill would not force railroads to convert many existing single-crew operations.

The railroads would bear new staffing costs, and a waiver provision lets carriers seek relief from the two-person rule, which supporters of one-person operations argue is unnecessary expense when technology like automated wayside signals can cover the safety functions of a second crew member.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core requirement — two qualified people on long or hazardous trains — is a straightforward safety measure, but the broad exceptions (yards, short moves, grandfathered single-crew operations, waivers) mean its real-world reach would be narrower than the headline. The main trade-off is railroad staffing costs against a second pair of trained hands on the trains carrying the most dangerous cargo.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to its railroads subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the Safe Freight Act on July 18, 2024, with one Republican cosponsor, Rep. Rulli of Ohio.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Class I freight railroads, which avoided a federal two-person crew mandate and its staffing costs. Rail workers and trackside communities gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: Rep. Michael Rulli
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only Republican support.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so partisan positions beyond the sponsorship itself — one Democrat and one Republican from Ohio — never surfaced.

industries.note: The bill would require them to staff most main line freight trains with a two-person crew, adding labor costs, with the strictest requirement on their longest and most hazardous trains. Because the bill died in committee, railroads avoid those costs. By keeping a public safety measure off the table at no cost to themselves, their interest ran against the workers and communities the bill aimed to protect.

Rail workers would gain a guaranteed second crew member on most main line trains, a safety and workload benefit, and had pushed for crew-size rules after a 2023 FRA proposal. Had it become law, their interest and the public's safety interest ran together.
